client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't bring myself to go, because being around everyone just makes her absence feel even more overwhelming. I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: I'm really glad you decided to reach out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying right now — the grief, the avoidance of those gatherings — makes a lot of sense given how much your grandmother must have meant to you. It takes courage to try talking when part of you isn't sure it will help, and that willingness itself matters. I'm curious — when you imagine being at one of those family get-togethers, what's the thought or feeling that feels most unbearable in that moment?

client: I think the most unbearable part is walking into a room where everyone is gathered around the table, and she's just... not there. It's like there's this huge empty space where she used to be, and everyone else seems to be coping or moving on, and I feel completely stuck and alone in it. And then I start feeling guilty, like maybe I should be stronger or more present for the rest of the family, but I just can't make myself do it.
therapist: That image of the empty space at the table is so painful, and it makes complete sense that you feel stuck when everyone around you seems to be moving at a different pace through their grief — grief isn't a race, and there's no "should" about how strong you need to be right now. I also notice you're carrying this guilt on top of the loss itself, which is such a heavy burden to hold alone. I'm wondering — where do you think that belief comes from, that you *should* be stronger or more present for others right now?

client: I think it probably comes from my grandmother herself, honestly. She was always the one holding everyone together, never falling apart, always showing up no matter what — and I guess I internalized that as the way you're supposed to be in this family. So now that she's gone, I feel like I should be stepping up somehow, but instead I'm the one hiding at home, which just makes me feel worse about myself.
therapist: It's deeply moving that the very person you're grieving is also the source of the standard you're holding yourself to — there's something really poignant and painful about that. I want to gently offer another perspective: perhaps the most honest way to honor someone who held everyone together is not to pretend you aren't hurting, but to allow yourself to grieve fully, because that grief itself is a testament to how much she meant to you. What do you think your grandmother would actually say if she could see you struggling right now — would she really demand that you be strong, or might she want something different for you?

client: Honestly, I know in my head that she would probably want me to be gentle with myself — she was never harsh with anyone, she was actually really warm and understanding. But it's hard to really feel that, because the moment I try to let myself off the hook, this voice kicks in that says I'm just making excuses for being weak or absent. I want to believe what you're saying, but I'm not sure knowing it in my head actually changes how it feels in my chest.
therapist: That gap between knowing something in your head and truly feeling it in your chest is one of the most frustrating parts of grief and self-criticism — and the fact that you can name it so clearly actually shows a lot of self-awareness. That harsh inner voice calling you "weak" sounds like it's been quite loud, and it's worth noticing that it doesn't actually sound anything like your grandmother, who you just described as warm and never harsh with anyone. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you grieving exactly the way you are right now, would you tell them they were being weak and making excuses?

client: No, of course I wouldn't say that to a friend — I'd probably sit with them and tell them it makes complete sense that they're struggling. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just feels different, like the rules are somehow different for me. I don't fully understand why I can extend that kind of compassion to other people so easily but the second it's directed inward it feels almost... undeserved.
therapist: That word "undeserved" is really important — it suggests this isn't just about grief, but that somewhere along the way you absorbed a belief that you are somehow less worthy of care and compassion than the people around you. That's a painful thing to carry, and it's worth exploring gently, because it's likely been there much longer than your grandmother's passing. What's your sense of where that feeling of not deserving the same kindness you'd give others might have come from?

client: That's a hard question, and I'm not sure I have a clean answer for it. I think growing up, I was always kind of the "responsible one" who had things together, and showing vulnerability felt like it would disappoint people or make me a burden — so I just learned to push through and keep it internal. My grandmother was actually one of the only people I felt safe being soft around, which maybe explains why losing her feels so destabilizing in a way that goes beyond just the grief itself.
therapist: What you just shared is really significant — your grandmother wasn't just someone you loved, she was one of the only safe places where you could put down that weight of always having to be "the one who has it together," and losing her means losing that sanctuary too. That helps explain why this grief feels so destabilizing, because it's not just about missing her presence, it's about losing the one relationship where you were allowed to be fully human and vulnerable. I'm wondering — as you sit with that realization, what does it bring up for you about what you might need most right now?

client: I think what I need most is exactly what I've lost — someone I can be a mess in front of without feeling like I'm letting them down or becoming a burden. But that realization is almost scarier than the grief itself, because I don't know if I have anyone else in my life where I feel that safe, and I'm not sure how you build that kind of trust with someone. It makes me feel lonelier than I expected to feel sitting here saying all of this out loud.
therapist: What you just named takes real courage to say out loud, and I want you to notice something — you came here unsure that talking would change anything, and yet you've just allowed yourself to be exactly the kind of "mess" you described, and the world didn't end, and you haven't burdened or disappointed me. That doesn't replace what you've lost, but it does suggest that the capacity to build that kind of safety with someone isn't gone, even if it feels very far away right now. I'm curious — what would it mean for you to consider that this space, right here, could be a small beginning of practicing exactly that?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me does notice that I've said more here than I've said to anyone in the past month, which is something. But I also find myself wondering if it feels safer precisely because you're not someone in my actual life — like, there are no stakes here the way there would be with a friend or family member who might look at me differently afterward. I want to believe this could be a beginning of something, but I'm honestly not sure how what happens in this room translates to the people I actually have to face at a family dinner.
therapist: You're making a really honest and insightful point — this space does feel lower stakes, and that's not a flaw, it's actually how trust often has to begin, in places where the risk feels manageable enough to practice being vulnerable at all. The goal wouldn't be to suddenly bare everything at a family dinner, but rather to use what you're discovering here — that you *can* let yourself be seen without falling apart — as something you slowly, gently test in small moments with the people in your life. I'm wondering, is there even one person in your life right now who might deserve a small chance, someone who's shown even a glimpse of that kind of warmth or safety?

client: There's maybe one person — my cousin, who was also really close to my grandmother and actually texted me a few weeks ago just to check in, and I never responded because I didn't know what to say. I keep thinking about reaching out but then I talk myself out of it, because what if she's coping better than me and I end up making her feel like she has to take care of me. I guess I'm worried that even a small step like that could go wrong in a way that leaves me feeling more alone than before.
therapist: It's really meaningful that your cousin reached out — and notice that she texted you first, which suggests she may be carrying her own grief and longing for exactly the kind of connection you're describing, someone who truly understood how special your grandmother was. The fear that you'll become a burden is that same old belief showing up again, but what if reaching out to her isn't you taking from her, but actually offering her something — the chance to grieve together with someone who loved your grandmother just as deeply? What do you think might happen if you simply responded to her message with something small and honest, not a full unburdening, just enough to open the door?

client: I think if I'm being honest, the idea of just sending something small feels slightly less terrifying than I expected it to when you put it that way — like maybe I don't have to have the perfect words or explain everything all at once. But I'm still scared that once I open that door even a little, she'll ask how I'm really doing and I won't be able to keep it contained, and then I'll have said too much and regret it. I guess I don't fully trust myself to know where the line is between opening up and just falling apart on her.
therapist: It's really encouraging that the idea of something small feels a little less terrifying — that shift matters, even if the fear is still there alongside it. I want to gently challenge the idea that "falling apart" in front of your cousin would automatically be a catastrophe — remember, she reached out because she cares, and you've already described her as someone close to your grandmother, which means she's probably not looking for you to be polished or contained. What if "saying too much" with her actually turned out to be the very thing you've both been quietly needing?
